topics: 🧱 The Stone, the Beam, and the Bathhouse Peruta — who becomes liable, and when
🏦 Shmuel Explains the Treasurer's Exemption — why holding consecrated property differs from transferring it
🪟 A Beam on the Windowsill — Rav's answer, and the deeper debate over attached vs. detached items
🍖 New Mishna: The Agent Who Swapped Meat for Liver — proper vs. improper performance of an errand
🐟 Why Fish, But Not Birds? — a detour through vows, bloodletting, and sore eyes to explain the mishna's examples

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Agency, Attachment, and the Limits of Liability
overview.subtitle: Meilah 20a–20b
overview.hebrewSource: הַשָּׁלִיחַ שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ – בַּעַל הַבַּיִת מָעַל. לֹא עָשָׂה שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ – הַשָּׁלִיחַ מָעַל
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through several scenarios testing exactly when benefit from consecrated property becomes me'ilah: giving a consecrated stone to another (only the giver is liable), building it into a wall (no liability until one lives beneath it), and paying a bathhouse attendant with consecrated money (liable immediately, even without bathing, since the option itself has value). The Gemara explores why a Temple treasurer is exempt while others aren't, and debates whether an item detached and then reattached to the ground still counts as 'detached' for me'ilah. A new mishna then opens a chapter on agency: if an agent properly carries out his errand, the one who sent him bears liability; if he deviates, the agent himself does — illustrated through a memorable case of swapped meat and liver at a dinner party.

slides.title: 🧱 Who's Liable, and When?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's chain of scenarios
rows: Took a consecrated stone/beam for himself
No one — not yet subject to me'ilah (attached-to-ground logic)
Gave that stone/beam to another person
The GIVER is liable; the recipient is not
Built the stone/beam into his own house
No one — until he actually resides beneath it and derives a peruta's worth of benefit
Took a consecrated peruta coin for himself
No one — not yet liable
Gave that peruta to another person
The GIVER is liable; the recipient is not
Gave the peruta to a bathhouse attendant (even without bathing)
The GIVER is liable immediately — the mere OPTION to enter and bathe is itself worth a peruta

slides.title: 🏦 Shmuel's Explanation: Why the Treasurer Is Different
slides.subtitle: Resolving why keeping an item is exempt but giving it away is not
slides.label: The answer:
slides.text: Why does simply taking the stone create no liability, while giving it to someone else does? Shmuel explains: the mishna's first clause describes a Temple TREASURER, to whom consecrated property is legitimately entrusted. Since holding the item is part of his job, mere possession isn't misuse — only once he TRANSFERS it beyond his official custody, to someone with no right to it, does me'ilah occur.

slides.title: 🪟 Rav's Windowsill and the Attached/Detached Debate
slides.subtitle: Does building consecrated material into a structure change its status?

nodes.content: ❓ Why does the mishna require actually LIVING beneath the beam? Doesn't shaping it to fit the building already count as 'change' (like idol worship requires)?
🔧 Rav: the case is a beam simply PLACED on a windowsill, unshaped — no 'change' occurred, so liability waits until real benefit (residing under it)
🏠 Does this support Rav's separate ruling that a house, though attached to the ground, still counts as 'detached' for idol-worship purposes (since it was built from detached materials)?

🔄 Rav Aḥa's alternative: even if attached material reverts to 'attached' status, misuse still applies here for a DIFFERENT reason — the Torah forbids any benefit 'visible to the eye,' regardless of attachment

✅ Reish Lakish's clarification of a supporting baraita: a house built from ALREADY-CONSECRATED materials stays subject to me'ilah; a house built first and consecrated AFTERWARD would not be (like the mishna's cave-dwelling exemption)

slides.title: 🍖 New Mishna: The Agent and the Swapped Dish
slides.subtitle: Proper agency shifts liability to the homeowner; deviation shifts it to the agent
rows: 'Give the guests meat'
Agent gave liver instead
The AGENT — he deviated from his instructions, so he acts on his own, not as an agent
'Give the guests liver'
Agent gave meat instead
The AGENT — same principle, reversed
'Give each guest one piece'
Agent said 'take two,' and guests took three
All three parties: homeowner (1st piece — instructions followed), agent (2nd piece — his own addition), guests (3rd piece — took beyond even the agent's word)

callout.label: Why meat vs. liver counts as deviation:
callout.text: Rav Ḥisda: this follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who treats liver, innards, and even bird meat as NOT the same category as ordinary meat — so substituting one for the other is a real deviation, not a minor adjustment an agent could reasonably make on his own.

slides.title: 🐟 A Detour: Why Are Birds Included but Fish Excluded?
slides.subtitle: Working out exactly which substitutions count as reasonable agency

lines.speaker: Question
lines.text: If a person naturally says 'I couldn't find animal meat, so I brought bird meat instead' (making birds an acceptable substitution an agent could make on his own) — wouldn't the same logic apply to fish?

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa (1st attempt)
lines.text: The case is the day of bloodletting, when people avoid fish for health reasons — so an agent would never even consider it.

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: But bloodletting also makes bird meat and salted meat inadvisable, per Shmuel and a baraita — so that reasoning proves too much!

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa (revised)
lines.text: Rather, the case is a day when the person's EYES hurt — fish are considered harmful for the eyes specifically, so an agent naturally wouldn't buy fish, while birds remain a sensible substitute.

callout.label: Final mishna note:
callout.text: Rav Sheshet reads the 'take two pieces' case narrowly: the agent explicitly said 'one piece per the homeowner's word, one per my own' — meaning the extra piece was clearly marked as the agent's OWN addition, not proof that any addition automatically counts as valid agency.

summary.principle: Me'ilah tracks who actually controls and benefits from consecrated property — a treasurer's custody isn't misuse, an agent's faithful errand shifts liability to the one who sent him, and even attachment to the ground doesn't shield 'visible benefit' from being treated as misuse.

flowSteps.content: 🧱 Stone/beam and peruta cases: giving triggers liability, mere possession or unshaped placement does not
🏦 Treasurer's custody is legitimate; transfer beyond it is where me'ilah begins
🪟 Attached-vs-detached debate resolved either through Rav's 'change' logic or Rav Aḥa's 'visible benefit' principle

columns.content: 🍖 Agent's proper errand → homeowner liable; deviation → agent liable
🐟 Reasonable substitutions (birds) differ from unreasonable ones (fish, liver) based on real-world custom

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability tracks true control and genuine benefit — technical attachment to land does not automatically exempt visible, real-world use

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, why is a Temple treasurer not liable for me'ilah merely for holding a consecrated stone or beam?
o: Because treasurers are exempt from all Temple laws
Because consecrated property is legitimately entrusted to his custody as part of his role; liability begins only once he transfers it to someone with no rightful claim to it
Because stones and beams are never subject to me'ilah
Because only priests can commit me'ilah
quiz.e: Shmuel explains that the mishna's case of 'no liability' describes a treasurer to whom the property is properly assigned; giving it away, beyond his legitimate custody, is what triggers me'ilah.

quiz.q: According to Rav, why does the mishna say one is not liable for a beam built into a house until he actually resides beneath it?
o: Because beams are never subject to me'ilah
Because the case involves a beam merely placed on a windowsill without being shaped or changed — so no 'change' has occurred yet to trigger liability
Because houses can never be consecrated
Because the mishna is discussing a different structure entirely
quiz.e: Rav explains that since the beam was placed, not altered or built into a wall, there's no 'change' (as idol worship comparisons require for damage-prone items) until actual residential benefit occurs.

quiz.q: What alternative principle does Rav Aḥa, son of Rav Ika, offer to explain liability for the beam case, regardless of the attached/detached debate?
o: That attachment to the ground makes no difference at all under normal circumstances
That the Torah forbids any benefit that is 'visible to the eye,' which applies here independent of whether the item counts as attached or detached
That only the treasurer can ever be liable
That beams are treated differently from stones
quiz.e: Rav Aḥa proposes that visible, apparent benefit is inherently forbidden by the Torah's me'ilah prohibition, sidestepping the entire question of whether reattached items revert to 'attached' status.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, who is liable for me'ilah if a homeowner instructs an agent to give guests meat, but the agent gives them liver instead?
o: The homeowner, since he gave the original instruction
The agent, since substituting liver for meat is a deviation from his agency, making him act independently rather than as an agent
The guests, since they consumed the item
No one is liable in this case
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that deviating from clear instructions (like swapping meat for liver) means the agent is no longer acting as an agent, so he personally bears the liability for misuse.

quiz.q: How does Rav Pappa ultimately explain why an agent could reasonably substitute bird meat for animal meat, but not fish?
o: Fish are never eaten by Jews
The scenario involves a day when the person's eyes hurt, and fish were considered harmful to the eyes, so an agent would not consider buying fish as a reasonable substitute, unlike birds
Birds are always more expensive than fish
There is no meaningful difference; the mishna is simply imprecise
quiz.e: After an initial answer about bloodletting was challenged (since bloodletting also restricts bird meat), Rav Pappa revises his explanation to a day when eating fish was considered harmful to the eyes specifically.
